title: How Black Holes Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain black holes: how they form when massive stars collapse (supernova or quiet collapse), the event horizon and singularity, stellar versus supermassive black holes, how gravity bends space and time, Schwarzschild and Kerr (rotating) types, the ergosphere, and how astronomers detect them indirectly through orbital motion, gravitational lensing, X-ray emission from accretion, and jets. They also cover Hawking evaporation, the quantum gravity problem, and a listener email about nuclear explosions in space.

segments.title: Opening banter and the question of seeing black holes
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the show's name and a YouTube series, then introduce the idea that black holes are invisible and that empiricism questions whether they can be known.

segments.title: History of prediction and definition of a black hole
segments.summary: Pierre-Simon Laplace calculated using Newtonian gravity that a compressed object could have escape velocity above light speed, long before Einstein. A black hole is what remains after a massive star collapses, via supernova or a quieter collapse.

segments.title: How stars balance fuel burning against gravity
segments.summary: A star is a fusion reactor where nuclear explosions push outward against gravity pulling inward. When fuel runs out, gravity wins and compresses the core, which becomes a very dense, small object with strong gravity that can sink into spacetime.

segments.title: Event horizon, orbits, and black hole movement
segments.summary: The event horizon is the boundary that swallows anything crossing it, though objects outside can orbit safely. Black holes can move through space, and they come in stellar (about 10 to 24 solar masses) and supermassive (millions to billions of solar masses) forms, with a supermassive one likely at the center of galaxies including the Milky Way.

segments.title: Time dilation near black holes and the Schwarzschild radius
segments.summary: Strong gravity bends spacetime and slows time near the event horizon. The Schwarzschild radius marks the event horizon size, named after Karl Schwarzschild; hosts estimate Earth would need to shrink to about marble size to become a black hole.

segments.title: Origin of supermassive black holes and rotating types
segments.summary: Discussion of how stellar black holes could merge or collide to form supermassive ones, and of Kerr rotating black holes versus Schwarzschild non-rotating ones, including the ergosphere and static limit and claims about singularities in rotating black holes and wormhole speculation.

segments.title: Detecting black holes indirectly
segments.summary: Black holes are detected through the motion of nearby objects (Kepler's third law and mass estimates), gravitational lensing confirmed in a solar eclipse test of Einstein's general relativity, brightening of stars from lensing, and X-rays from accretion and jets.

segments.title: Black hole lifespan, size, and unsolved questions
segments.summary: Hawking showed black holes slowly evaporate, rather than lasting forever. Event horizon sizes range from about six miles to the size of the solar system. Inside a black hole is unknown; quantum gravity is an unsolved problem in physics.

segments.title: Hubble site resource and book recommendation
segments.summary: Hosts recommend Hubble site's black hole resources and discuss the novel The Man Who Folded Himself, along with brief talk of The Hunger Games.

segments.title: Listener mail on nukes in space
segments.summary: Mark from New Jersey writes that Michio Kaku said nuclear weapons do not work in space because there are no atoms to transfer energy, and the hosts discuss nuclear testing in space.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to share their own smart stories and give social media and email contacts.
